subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: Hello. I'm a woman, and I'm here because I hurt my right ankle yesterday when I slipped on ice. I can't walk on it very well and it's been pretty painful. Doctor: Could you please provide your age and describe the injury to your right ankle in more detail, including when it occurred, how it happened, and what symptoms you're currently experiencing? Patient: I'm 35, and I hurt my ankle yesterday when I was taking out the trash. It was really icy, and I slipped and fell. I think I heard a pop when I landed, and I couldn't walk on it at all at first. Now I can put a little weight on it, but I'm still limping. It's been pretty painful, but the ibuprofen helps a bit. Patient: I've had a lot of ankle injuries before, but I've never hurt this specific ankle before. I just realized that now. Patient: I haven't noticed any numbness or tingling in my foot, and the skin color and temperature feel normal. There is some bruising on the outside of my ankle and it's swollen, but I don't see any deformity. Doctor: Could you describe the range of motion of your right ankle? Are you able to move it up and down, side to side, or is there any restriction? Patient: I can move my ankle a little bit, but it's really restricted. It's hard to move it up and down or side to side without pain, and I definitely can't bear much weight on it. It feels pretty stiff and sore when I try to move it

The patient has a history of multiple ankle injuries, which increases the likelihood of ligamentous damage. Other differentials include soft tissue injury and possible early-stage osteochondral injury, which may not be visible on plain X-ray. A high ankle sprain or subtle stress fracture is less likely given the absence of significant tenderness over the syndesmosis and the negative X-ray.
